newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Barges gridlocked by record IPE gas oil delivery.
newsitem.headline: Barges gridlocked by record IPE gas oil delivery.

text.p: Barges in Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp (ARA) are stuck in queues and others have been sent on wild goose chases in their hunt for gas oil to supply this month's record IPE delivery, charterers and traders said on Monday.
"It's ridiculous. There's lots of queues, lots of barges waiting and no oil (readily available)," said one Dutch barge charterer.
Some charterers are already saying the task of delivering up to 800,000 tonnes of gas oil cannot be completed by the end of the month. One said some loadings may be delayed until December 10.
The IPE contract specifies delivery in 16-30 November, but the parties can also agree to alternative delivery procedures (ADP), usually involving a cash element.
The IPE declined to comment: "It would be inappropriate to discuss anything before the end of the delivery window," said Richard Ward, executive vice-president of business development.

The delivery against the expired November IPE futures contract was to have started in earnest on Saturday and charterers say that many of their barges should by now have completed their third trip. A number have not even begun the outward leg of their first journey.
One charterer said some of his barges had shuttled between two storage facilities in Amsterdam in a fruitless search for oil.
Another said barges were waiting behind sea-going vessels, the loading of which was well behind schedule.

Last Tuesday, the IPE said the delivery against the expired November gas oil contract would be at a record high, of 865,100 tonnes, beating the previous peak of 853,600 tonnes set in January. Deliveries in the last two weeks of January proved difficult, although the task began a little more promisingly then.
"Obviously, it's an enormous job within a very short space of time and there's plenty scope for congestion in loading and discharging," said Dutch oil consultant Pieter Kulsen.
This month's delivery is believed to be going almost exclusively to one company, Cargill, from another trader, AIC, but sources at these companies declined to comment.

Traders said some of the total was probably destined for Asia, but much will have to stay in the ARA market and the Rhine system. With weakness in Asia on Monday morning, traders speculated that about 50 percent will stay in local markets.
Barge rates in the ARA area are up about 40 percent, although some charterers are finding it hard to find any spare vessels at all.

When they can, they are only prepared to quote day rates, rather than rates per tonne. Charterers reason that their barges will probably have to sit in queues at storage facilities. Rates per tonne do not normally include payments for delays.
Even so, charterers are disgruntled with the log-jam.
"We only make a profit when we are moving. We make nothing from these delays," one charterer said.
